title: Where to Fly Fish in Wine Country, According to the Pros
summary:
Wine and fly fishing have more in common than you think. Here are the best places to do both.

The post Where to Fly Fish in Wine Country, According to the Pros appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The fishing line unfurls behind you. You gently push your arm and fishing rod forward and let the line unwind. It gracefully lands atop the river without making a ripple. Then, a mouth rises from the water and snatches the fly, you pull back on the line and feel a sharp tug—this is fly fishing.

While nationwide participation remains relatively low, fly fishing is slowly increasing in popularity. According to the American Sportfishing Association’s Special Report on Fishing in 2025, the number of fly fishers in the United States has increased by over 2 million participants compared to a decade prior. 

Any wine lovers interested in exploring fly fishing already have a leg up—the two have more in common than you may think. Finding success on the river requires patience and appreciation for the environment around you, much like enjoying or producing an exceptional bottle of wine. This synergy makes fly fishing in wine country the perfect pairing.

Whether you’re an avid oenophile, a passionate fly fisher, or both, here are some of the best regions to enjoy a glass and hook a giant. 

Please be advised that hiking out to and wading into rivers can be dangerous. Research all regions and bodies of water before heading out. Also, you’ll need a permit to fish in certain rivers.

The Hudson Valley/Catskills, New York

While sometimes disputed, the Catskills, located in Central New York, is often called the birthplace of American fly fishing.

“As it developed in the 1800s, we became the most popular location, and indeed, many of the innovations of those early years occurred in our area,” says Paul T. “Terry” Shultz, a former board member of the Catskill Fly Fishing Center and Museum. Shultz has fished the Catskills since the 1950s.

Early innovators in the region included Theodore Gordon, who revolutionized dry fly fishing (a version where a dry fly sits on the surface of the water instead of sinking); Reuben Cross, who shaped how flies are tied; and Joan Wulff, who reshaped casting techniques and founded a fly fishing school in the Catskills that continues to operate today.

While there’s an abundance of rivers and other bodies of water to fish, some of the best known trout rivers, according to Shultz, include the Beaver Kill, the Willowemoc, the Neversink, the Esopus, and the Schoharie—”these five comprise the ‘Charmed Circle,’” he says. “Plus, the Delaware and its two branches, the East and West.”

About an hour south of the Neversink River, you’ll find the 80-mile-long Shawangunk Wine Trail, which runs throughout Ulster and Orange counties in the Mid-Hudson Valley region and includes 13 wineries and cideries, such as Whitecliff Vineyard, Magnanini Farm Winery, and Angry Orchard’s Cider House.

Lewis-Clark Valley, Idaho

Home to the Snake River, Clearwater River, and more than 50 wineries, Idaho is the place to be for fly fishing wine lovers. Much like the Catskills, the Gem State has a long history with the sport.

“Because of its remoteness and access to high-mountain lakes and streams, Idaho became a fly-fishing destination during the sport’s boom between the 1930s and 1960s,” says Connor Jay Liess, public information specialist at the Idaho Department of Fish and Game. “Well-known public figures such as Ernest Hemingway and even presidents made trips out to Idaho to fish its scenic rivers and streams.”

Idaho is home to three American Viticulture Areas (AVAs): Eagle Foothills, Snake River Valley, and Lewis-Clark Valley. The latter is a favorite of many fly fishers.

“Every year, thousands of folks flock to the Lewis-Clark Valley to fly fish along its scenic rivers and mountain streams,” says Liess. “Lewiston sits in a pretty unique geographic spot in Idaho where the Snake River meets the Clearwater River. Both rivers offer several access sites, spectacular views, and unrivaled opportunities to catch both steelhead and salmon during the colder months, typically September through December.”

Andrew “Drew” Evans, manager at the House of Fly shop in Lewiston, also recommends the Clearwater River for steelhead and notes that fishers can possibly catch smallmouth bass and carp on the Snake River.

While you’re there, be sure to check out the AVA’s eight wineries. Grapes have been planted in the region since at least the 1870s. And the Lewis-Clark AVA produces notable Cabernet Sauvignon, along with Riesling, Tempranillo, and more.

Rangeley Lakes Region, Maine

Home to more than 3,000 miles of coastline—one of the largest in the nation—there’s no shortage of places in Maine to explore, especially if fly fishing and wine are on the itinerary.

Michelle Landry, executive director of Historic Rangeley, notes that earliest inhabitants of the Americas and the ancestors of today’s Wabanaki fished Maine’s extensive bodies of water long before European settlers arrived.

But the fishing industry in Maine’s Rangeley region changed in 1863 when George Shepard Page, a businessman from New York, was so “impressed with his Rangeley fishing experience, that he sent eight brook trout he caught to editors of the New York Times, the New York Evening Post, and the Spirit of the Times,” says Landry.

After the “secret was out, more anglers started visiting the Rangeley Lakes region to fish for the famous brook trout,” says Landry. “Hotels, lodges, and sporting camps sprung up around the area to accommodate visitors who wanted to try their hand at catching a record-breaking Maine brook trout.”

For water in Western Maine, Landry notes that the Rapid River, Upper Dam Pool, Magalloway River, Kennebago River, and the Lower Cupsuptic are “known for trophy-size wild brook trout and wild landlocked salmon and are open to fly fishing only,” she says.

After a day on the water, you can check out some of the 15 wineries on the Maine Wine Trail.

“The wine industry is growing exponentially, with new producers and vineyards popping up every year,” says Margot Mazur, wine writer and educator at The Fizz.

But when traveling down the Maine Wine Trail, don’t expect large wineries.

“Maine is mostly made up of smaller vineyards and producers,” says Mazur. “You won’t find many large commercial vineyards in this area, and we’re okay with that. It’s a small community of passionate people and farmers. We’ll be happy to welcome you!”

Grand Junction, Colorado

Home to four national parks and countless miles of river, there’s no shortage of places to explore and get your waders wet in the Centennial State.

If you’re looking to enjoy a glass of something local after a day on the water, head to Grand Junction, Colorado, which is about four hours west of Denver.

Tyler Morris, founder of Drift Boat Taroon Club and a guide at Western Anglers in Grand Junction, leads guided float trips on the lower section of the Colorado River (from Colorado’s Glenwood Springs to Rifle), and a three-day, two-night camping trip down Gunnison Gorge (starting at the Chukar Trail and ending at Pleasure Park).

He notes that the Gunnison is “actually one of the steepest rivers in the continental United States. It’s got the most gradients [and] it’s very, very fast [with] lots of rapids.” So, it’s best to book a guided trip, like with Western Anglers.

While fishing both bodies of water is different, Morris notes that “they’re pretty healthy, wild rivers. There are good wild populations. They don’t stock any of the brown trout. So, every brown trout that you catch is completely wild.”

Along with wild brown trout, you could also possibly catch rainbows, cutthroats, and the Colorado River cutthroat, which is its own subspecies of trout. There are also the native flannelmouth suckers, bluehead suckers, and white fish.

On the stretch of the Colorado River, Morris notes that you can see cottonwood trees, and possibly bald eagles. Whereas on that stretch of the Gunnison, it’s 2,000 feet from the river to the rim of the canyon.

“It’s kind of breathtaking, as corny as that sounds” says Morris. “A lot of people, when we are fishing, I tell them, ‘just take a minute and look up at the canyon walls.’ You’ll see these rock formations that are just so old and just crazy to think that a river formed them.”

Along with ample rivers, Grand Junction is also home to the Grand Valley AVA, where you’ll find more than 30 wineries. While a host of grapes are planted throughout the state, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, and Riesling are the dominant varieties.

title: This Chic Roman Bar Is Basically an Art Museum with Cocktails
summary:
Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace is an art history lover’s dream, without the tickets and crowds of most Roman haunts.

The post This Chic Roman Bar Is Basically an Art Museum with Cocktails appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The amount of art to see in Rome is overwhelming. Over 20 Caravaggio paintings hang in churches, museums, and palaces scattered throughout the city. The Sistine Chapel awaits only those who sweat through an hours-long queue (or pay fees to skip the line.) But one unassuming yet glamorous bar, in the lobby of a hotel perched on the city’s highest hilltop, is a museum in and of itself.

With three masterpieces from Giovanni Battista Tiepolo and countless rare paintings, sculptures, furniture, and tapestries, Rome Cavalieri’s Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace is an art history lover’s dream, without the tickets and crowds of most Roman haunts.

Even if you’re not staying overnight in one of the hotel’s palatial suites, many of which house art themselves—an original painting from Andy Warhol’s Dollar Sign series hangs in the penthouse—you can visit Tiepolo for aperitivo and soak in all the art history. The ornate, elegant bar is open to the public and even hosts tours guided by local art historians.

The Decor

Rome Cavalieri, a Waldorf Astoria hotel, houses one of the more impressive private art collections in the world, with over a thousand rare and historic pieces displayed throughout the hotel. The most notable paintings hang near the lobby’s elegant Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace, named after the three Giovanni Battista Tiepolo masterpieces displayed on the wall beside the bar. Known for his frescoes and Rococo style, the Venice-born artist is considered one of the most important painters of the 18th century.

The three large canvases—the only pieces at Rome Cavalieri behind glass, due to their preciousness—include “Odysseus finds Achilles among the daughters of Lycomedes,” “The Flaying of Marsyas,” and “Hercules and Antaeus.”

Secure your spot now.

Guests can sip their aperitivo from the cozy antique furniture that surrounds the sleek bar while gazing upon the 18th-century Tiepolo paintings, or the large tapestry of “L’Histoire de l’Empereur de Chine,” replicas of which hang at the Louvre, the Met, and the Getty Museum. Frequent live harp and piano performances elevate the classic atmosphere even further, and terrace seating offers sweeping views of the hotel’s Mediterranean gardens and the Rome cityscape.

The Drinks

In addition to all the aperitivo classics you would expect from a Roman bar—spritzes, martinis, and bitter sodas abound—the Tiepolo menu features a thoughtful collection of art-inspired cocktails that take cues from the property’s most prominent works. The signature Tiepolo cocktail is an aromatic, gently bitter gin and grapefruit treat, while A…Dollar, inspired by the penthouse’s original Warhol, is a vanilla-scented vodka sour riff. 

There is also an impressive assortment of zero-proof options, as well, including my personal favorite, the refreshing Vermeil 0%, made with Sabatini 0% gin and herbal Tassoni cedrata soda. Between 3:30 and 5:30 p.m., the lounge offers a dedicated high tea service, with finger sandwiches and freshly baked sweet treats like madeleines and mini plum cakes.

The Crowd

Expect to see relaxed guests enjoying a glamorous pre-dinner aperitivo, or more casual business meetings over coffee (or high tea service) earlier in the day. The bar is open to the general public and typically has ample seating available without reservations. 

The Bottom Line

For world-famous art with top-tier cocktails to match, Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace offers a singular experience in Rome. Despite the seriousness of the surrounding artwork, Tiepolo feels welcoming, warm, and relaxed.

Why Portugal Is One of the World’s Most Exciting Wine Regions

What wine should you open with dinner? The answer, regardless of what’s on the table, is Portuguese.

Within the country’s confines, you can find a whole globe of styles to match every meal, be it large or small, snack-y or stretched into several courses. With over 250 native grape varieties and a wild diversity of wine regions, Portuguese wines have range.

“In a wine world that often speaks through a familiar handful of international varieties, Portugal has preserved an entire native vocabulary,” says Master Sommelier June Rodil, partner and CEO of Goodnight Hospitality. “Arinto’s salt, citrus, and electric acidity; Encruzado’s layered, quietly powerful texture; Touriga Nacional’s perfume and architecture; Baga’s yummy yet haunting, savory grip.”

The Rich Diversity of Portuguese Wine

The expressive red wines of the Douro Valley complement savory dishes like grilled tuna steak, spiced curry, or winter braises. In the summer months, brighter reds made from the Baga grape, grown on Bairrada’s coast, or Castelão from the hills outside Lisboa play well with low-key pizzas, grilled skewers, or platters of cheeses, olives, and meats. 

Touriga Nacional, arguably Portugal’s most iconic grape, is revered for its structure and elegant perfumes. In the Douro, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinta Amerela (i.e. Trincadeira), and Touriga Franca all offer their own unique brand of liveliness, structure, and spice to blends.

Freshness-seekers have a lot to love in the country’s white varieties. Found both in blends and single-variety wines, the vibrant acidity of the Arinto grape or the aromatic character of Loureiro, which hails from the North West, cut through the crunch of fried fritters and elevate crisp salad. Globally-popular Alvarinho is known for precision and intensity, while Encruzado, found in the Dão, brings texture to a blend. 

“These grapes can be beautiful on their own, but many are at their most compelling in a convo with one another, building complexity through contrast rather than sheer weight,” says Rodil. 

Portugal’s excellence goes well beyond still reds and whites. The sparkling wines of Bairrada are full of energy and an oceanic acidity. And of course, Port, one of the world’s most iconic wines, and Madeira, a fortified island wine, need little introduction.

This variety of styles, native grapes, and expressions mean that there’s a whole country to discover. And more wine stories to unravel around every corner. 

“You aren’t tasting a Portuguese grape trying to fit a global mold; you’re tasting place, history, and personality, all speaking with a distinctly Portuguese accent,” Rodil adds.

Structured Reds of the Douro

The extreme, rugged slopes of the Douro Valley is home to hundreds of unique varieties and an extensive array of old vines. From the slopes and xisto (schist) soil surrounding the river come wines of structure, power, and finesse. 

Touriga Nacional—one of Portugal’s most emblematic varieties—brings aromatics and concentration to the Douro’s signature red blends. Other indigenous red grapes like Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, and Tinta Amarela all add their own unique characteristics to the mix. Their diverse aromas and textures give winemakers space to play and to build the perfect blend.

Expressive Alentejo

While the Douro’s landscapes are dramatic, Alentejo is mostly a region of gently rolling plains dotted with oak and cork trees. An overarching quality of both the reds and whites is freshness—surprising considering the sundrenched summer days that bless the region. 

With a 2,000-year-old history of viticulture, Alentejo is home to a number of beloved varieties. Alicante Bouschet is the star in the region’s iconic red blends. Aragonez (Tempranillo) brings structure and elegance. Juicy Castelão is often added into blends for its red fruit aromas. Likewise, Trincadeira, for its plummy, savory notes, while Moreto is recognized for its low acidity and nuttiness. And Arinto brings lemon-lime brightness to refreshing white blends.

Refreshing Vinhos Verdes

The salty Atlantic air and the cool ocean breezes make the Vinhos Verdes wine region one of the most distinctive growing areas in Portugal. White grapes, including Alvarinho, Arinto (Pedernã, to the locals), Azal, Avesso, Loureiro, and Trajadura is blended into aromatic, fresh, verdant wines that shine when paired with seafood or dishes with big spice, bright citrus, or an herbaceous kick.

Elegant Dão

Surrounded by mountains in all directions, Dão is one of the oldest regions in Portugal. Touriga Nacional, the region’s star, brings to life age-worthy blends with full body and great alcohol content. Open a bottle with a rib-eye or cold-weather braises, like Caçoila, a warming stewed beef dish. 

Don’t overlook the region’s other grapes. Tinta Pinheira, also known as Rufete, has an incredible depth of color and complexity. Encruzado, a noble white grape, with lively lemon aromas.

Bouncy Bairrada

Hugging the coast and defined by Atlantic influence, Bairrada is known for its cool, sea-kissed climate.

Two styles shine here: the fierce tannins and springy saltiness of single-variety Baga, with its wild fruit and early minerality, and Portuguese’s finest sparkling wines, born from centuries-old vines in sandy soils by the sea and bursting with tension, aromatics, and ocean salinity.

Beyond Baga and bubbles, white grapes like Fernão Pires (or, Maria Gomes), Arinto, Bical, and Cercial tend to take on a striking mineral character.

Surfer Cool Lisboa

Lisboa’s wines are made between the cool winds of the Atlantic ocean and the sunny heat of inland Portugal. Sun and surf define wines—maritime influence, morning fog, ocean breezes, and white wines full of seaside minerality. Reds range from structured and powerful to easy-drinking and beachy. That vibrant acidity will cut through fat and spice—be it from pho or larb, or comfy Southern flavors.

Península de Setúbal

One of the country’s most prestigious regions is also the birthplace of Moscatel de Setúbal, a rich, aromatic fortified sweet wine. With a richly Mediterranean climate, the red wines of the Palmela region, based on the Castelão grape variety, have complexity, depth, and extreme ageability.

“Portuguese wine can move through an entire menu, from something bracing and oceanic to something structured and deeply soulful, while remaining unmistakably itself,” Rodil adds. “For a sommelier, that range is what makes these wines so badass.”

title: Collecting Chartreuse Is a Spiritual Contradiction. Somms Do It Anyway
summary:
Chartreuse sustains the lives of the monks who make it, yet they refuse to exploit its value fully. Still, the liqueur inspires a frenzy among collectors.

The post Collecting Chartreuse Is a Spiritual Contradiction. Somms Do It Anyway appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At the end of a great wine dinner, when the bottles stand empty and the table has fallen into the pleasant disorder of stained glasses and dismantled cheese plates, Paul Einbund reaches for Chartreuse.

“I can be completely taken by the wines, but when I pour Chartreuse afterward, I remember how deeply it affects me,” says Einbund. He’s the owner of San Francisco restaurants The Morris and Sirene, as well as the coauthor, with Jordan Mackay, of the forthcoming Little Green Book of Chartreuse. “Made from 130 herbs and plants, it’s just more complex than anything else. There is mystery and drama in the glass!”

For years, this was Einbund’s private passion, when all Chartreuse did was gather dust on liquor store shelves, and many dismissed it as an eccentric digestif or a formidable ingredient in old cocktails. Then bartenders rediscovered drinks such as the Last Word, and sommeliers began pouring vintage bottles after dinner. Soon the spirits world’s trending fascination grew into something approaching mania.

From Mythic Origins to Collector Obsession

Chartreuse begins with 130 plants, herbs, roots, barks, seeds, and spices. Around half, by volume, come from the French and Italian Alps, according to Philippe Rochez, sales director of Chartreuse Diffusion. Others arrive from farther away. All are delivered dried to the Grande Chartreuse monastery in France, where secrecy is maintained with almost theatrical rigor.

Only two monks know the complete recipe and its precise proportions. A third knows the ingredients and inspects each shipment as it arrives. Before passing the invoices to the accountant, this monk uses a black marker to obscure what has been ordered. The company may pay for the plants and spices, but its accountants are not permitted to know what they are.

The monks combine the botanicals inside the monastery, placing them into coded bags before they are sent for distillation. Different proportions and methods produce Green Chartreuse, Yellow Chartreuse, and the powerful Élixir Végétal. The liqueurs are sweetened with French beet sugar and aged in oak vessels ranging from barriques to enormous vats. Chartreuse Diffusion buys new barrels to avoid foreign aromas and refuses to sell retired ones for use by other producers.

Time brings the alcohol, sugar, and plants together. Older Green Chartreuse can evoke pine, smoke, tea, and peppercorn. Yellow, made at a lower strength and with different proportions, can turn toward ginger, cardamom, saffron, and dried fruit.

This complexity helps explain its appeal to sommeliers. Einbund considers Chartreuse through much the same framework he applies to wine: weight, acidity, balance, intensity, and density. He drinks it differently, however.

“Because of the higher alcohol levels, I sip by taking a little more than wetting my lips, and I almost let it evaporate on my palate,” he says. “This way I can slow things down and watch the flavors expand as I enjoy them, and avoid the burn at the same time.”

Its evolution in bottle has also created a passionate collector culture. Vintage-spirits consultant Seth Weinberg began accumulating Chartreuse after tasting several releases together. “Many years ago after trying multiple vintages of Chartreuse side by side, I noticed the nuanced differences in various vintages,” Weinberg says. “This realization led to a natural urge to collect.”

His approach resembles building a wine cellar: buy each release when it appears, then wait. “Since Chartreuse ages like a wine in the bottle, I believe it is paramount to buy bottles when they are released, and age them for many years for the flavors to develop, oxidize, and harmonize,” he says.

The trophies include a 1953 VEP made to commemorate the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, the original ninth-centenary bottling from 1984, and a three-liter carbon-fiber Jeroboam released in 2019 and limited to 999 bottles. Weinberg bought the Jeroboam at the distillery in France and carried it throughout the country, its weight wearing down the rubber on his suitcase wheels against the cobblestones.

Yet collecting Chartreuse contains a spiritual contradiction. The Carthusians do not live on donations. They support themselves through their work, with revenue through Chartreuse Diffusion helping sustain the order and its monasteries. They make liqueur to preserve their independence and a life devoted to silence, solitude, and prayer—not to build a global liquor empire.

The Mystery and Mythology of a Sacred Spirit

“All winemakers like Chartreuse,” says Rochez, who has spent 38 years at Chartreuse Diffusion, his first and only employer. He sees a kinship between winegrowers and the monks. Both work with plants, depend upon nature, and allow time to finish what they began. Climate change is complicating that work, Rochez says, as some herbs become drier and others more difficult to source.

Chartreuse’s history has demanded similar patience. The liqueur takes its name from the Chartreuse Mountains, where Saint Bruno founded the Carthusian order in 1084. The Carthusians received a manuscript for an “elixir of long life” in 1605 and spent more than 150 years refining it. The liqueur survived revolution; the monks’ expulsion from France; production in Tarragona, Spain; the destruction of the distillery in Fourvoirie, France; and periods when few people seemed to want it.

Einbund believes the enigma and mythology surrounding Chartreuse is central to its hold over sommeliers. Wine professionals spend their lives studying provenance, production, and vintage, but Chartreuse keeps part of itself hidden. 

“One of the most important lessons for me about Chartreuse is to let go of trying to be right, or know everything,” he says. “Chartreuse is a mystery and always will be. That’s part of what makes it so amazing.”

Demand for Chartreuse began surging during the cocktail renaissance of the early 2000s, fueled by the revival of the Last Word, and accelerated further with the rise of home mixology during the pandemic. But the monks refused to keep increasing production simply because the market would absorb it. According to Rochez, they now make more Chartreuse than they did for much of the past several decades, but have stabilized output to protect their monastic life.

Bottles consequently disappear, allocations tighten, and prices climb. What once gathered dust is now hoarded, traded, and displayed behind glass. This troubles the monks, who believe Chartreuse should be opened and shared, not treated as a speculative asset.

Weinberg understands the contradiction. “I share the same sentiment as the monks,” he says. “Bottles of liquor are best enjoyed when opened and shared.”

Perhaps this is what sommeliers recognize most clearly. Every extraordinary bottle arrives with the knowledge that opening it destroys the object that has been guarded. Chartreuse asks for that surrender more forcefully than most. Conceived as an “elixir of long life,” it now sustains the lives of the monks who make it, yet they refuse to exploit its value fully. They will produce enough to preserve their way of life, but not enough to satisfy our appetite. 

Back at Einbund’s table, poured after the last wine, its purpose becomes clear. Chartreuse slows the evening down, giving its flavors and the conversation around them time to expand. Perhaps that is why it affects him so deeply: The liqueur was never meant to live behind glass, but among the people gathered around it.

Celebrate Fall with a Four-Course Italian Alpine Dinner Party

A taste of Trentino, without leaving home.

Imagine an autumn evening in the Italian Alps: crisp mountain air, a full table of seasonal dishes, toasting friends, a complete sense of presence. Make that vision a reality with this Italian Alpine Dinner Party.

Rooted in the dramatic landscapes of Trentino, Italy, where vineyards climb the foothills of the Dolomites and cool alpine conditions preserve freshness and acidity, Mezzacorona and Rotari wines capture the freshness, elegance, and distinctive character of their region. 

These wines take center stage across an inspired four-course, fall menu. Each pairing brings something different to the table, starting with the Rotari Brut and Rotari Brut Rosé, both crafted in the Alps using the traditional bottle-fermentation technique that gives the lively sparkling wines their fine bubbles, freshness, complexity, and refined texture.  The experience then moves into the still wines of Trentino, from the fresh, mineral precision of Domenica Pinot Grigio to the juicy, expressive character of DiNotte Red Blend

Consider this your invitation to slow down, savor each glass, and enjoy the Italian art of gathering one delicious course at a time.

Explore the Wines

Welcome Aperitivo

Rotari Brut Trentodoc

title: With Over 100,000 Bottles, This Basque Cellar Is Like a Museum for Wine Lovers
summary:
Rekondo’s 376-page wine list spans more than 20 countries and reflect the founder's passion for Rioja, Burgundy, and Basque Country wines.

The post With Over 100,000 Bottles, This Basque Cellar Is Like a Museum for Wine Lovers appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
On the top of a hill at the edge of La Concha Bay in San Sebastián, Spain, you’ll find Rekondo, a quaint family-run restaurant that has served traditional Basque cuisine since 1964. 

Its founder, Txomin Rekondo, is an avid oenophile, ever in search of wines that pair with the restaurant’s dishes. During his travels throughout Spain and France in the ’60s, he purchased bottles at a rate that quickly outgrew the storage capabilities at Rekondo.

So, in 1970, to accommodate this growing collection, Rekondo dug a cellar beneath the restaurant to store and protect wine from the elements. Today, that collection has grown to more than 100,000 bottles from over 20 countries. Its exceptional breadth, deep holdings of Rioja and Burgundy, and carefully maintained historic vintages have earned Rekondo recognition as one of the world’s great restaurant cellars.

The Design

The underground cellar at Rekondo is divided into three rooms, each housing white wines, reds, and historic bottles. Lourdes Rekondo, Txomin’s daughter and the restaurant’s general manager, renovated portions of the cellar about five years ago. The cellar’s entrance is new and polished, with backlit racks of white wines and glass display cases showcasing some of the owner’s most impressive bottles. During the redesign, the white wines were moved into the renovated area, while the reds were considered too delicate to disturb. 

Inside, tastings and special events are hosted in a private, modern dining room near the cellar entrance. The dining room features elegant place settings, two crystal chandeliers over the table, and large windows that let in natural light. Much of the original cellar remains intact, with many bottles still in their original locations. 

The cellar’s dense rows, low lighting, large-format bottles, and rare vintages from across generations make it feel more like a historical archive than a typical restaurant storeroom. Its largest chamber contains roughly 80,000 bottles arranged in numbered wooden bins according to Txomin’s organizational system, with clear plastic wrap protecting the oldest labels. “It’s not very elegant, but it works,” Lourdes says. 

The Collection

Rekondo’s 376-page wine list spans more than 20 countries and reflects Txomin’s particular passion for wine from the Rioja and Burgundy areas. Historic Spanish holdings include a vertical of Imperial and collections of Vega Sicilia and Marqués de Riscal, including an 1880 Marqués de Riscal—one of the cellar’s oldest bottles. 

French producers represented in the collection include Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, one of Burgundy’s most coveted names; Bordeaux First Growths Château Latour, Château Margaux, and Château Lafite Rothschild; and Château d’Yquem, the only Sauternes estate ranked Premier Cru Supérieur in the 1855 classification. Together, they reflect the collection’s depth in some of France’s most historic, ageworthy, and sought-after wines. 

Champagne, Port, and wines from Priorat also appear throughout the cellar, many of them in magnum and larger formats. Local identity comes through txakoli and reds from Rioja Alavesa, the subregion located within the Basque Country. Txakoli is a natural match for oysters, clams, hake, and lobster, while Rioja Alavesa reds complement the menu’s heartier dishes such as venison, suckling pig, filet mignon, and rib-eye.

Why It Stands Out

Despite its museum-caliber holdings, Rekondo treats wine as something to drink rather than collect and preserve indefinitely. “Our policy is that we want to sell to buy more,” Lourdes says. Even bottles that remain in single quantities may be opened, but only for true oenophiles—people their team believes will truly appreciate the wine.

Many have signed empty bottles that are displayed throughout the cellar, marking shared celebrations. For example, Txomin opened a Romanée-Conti after golfer José María Olazábal won his first Masters in 1994, while an enormous bottle of Alión was poured for Real Sociedad football players after a major win. 

Some of the cellar’s greatest treasures remain hidden for protection, and Lourdes says even she doesn’t know where they are (only her father does). Ultimately, she says, the cellar’s prevailing philosophy is one of generosity: “My father always said that the wine is to share.”

There once was a time when Advent calendars were filled with little cardboard illustrations, or, if you were lucky, cardboard-tasting chocolates. Thankfully, we have entered the golden era of Advent calendars, filled with legitimately exciting gifts: jams, lipsticks, teas, perfumes, macarons, and, best of all, booze. 

For the uninitiated, Advent calendars can be any shape or size, but they always feature 24 to 25 “doors” meant to be opened every day leading up to Christmas, revealing a festive surprise. (There are also 12-day versions that count down to Christmas.) The item has its roots in 19th-century Germany, where Protestants began counting down to Christmas by lighting candles or making marks with chalk on walls or doors. It is believed that the first chocolate-filled Advent calendars emerged in the 1950s, and Cadbury launched its own in 1971.

The lavish themed Advent calendars of today—often exorbitantly priced, like the controversial $825 Chanel Advent calendar of 2021—are a far cry from its humble origins. (We’re not sure how 19th-century German Protestants would respond to the sight of a “24 Days of Rum” Advent calendar, but we suspect they wouldn’t love it.) 

In the lead-up to this holiday season, give the gift of adult beverages. Whatever your loved ones like to drink, whether it’s wine, spirits, beer, or liqueurs, there’s a calendar for it. These are the 13 best boozy Advent calendars we could find this year.

title: Central Coast Innovator Gretchen Roddick Is Wine Enthusiast’s Person of the Year
summary:
The executive vice president of Hope Family Wines has helped shape the Central Coast wine scene for decades.

The post Central Coast Innovator Gretchen Roddick Is Wine Enthusiast’s Person of the Year appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
As the daughter of two blue-collar entrepreneurs, Gretchen Roddick learned early on what it takes to succeed in any industry.   

“You work hard, fail fast, then get up and do it again,” said Roddick, who is being honored with the Wine Star Award for Person of the Year. “I really take pride in the work ethic I was taught growing up.”

No surprise that the executive vice president of Hope Family Wines and board chair of the Wine Institute started working at age 14. “There’s never been a day that I haven’t had a job,” said Roddick.

Initially starting as a tasting-room host for Hope Family back in 1997, she’s helped the company grow from just 1,000 cases of wine to nearly one million today, which are distributed in all 50 states and 62 countries. Among numerous other volunteer positions, she joined the Wine Institute—which promotes California wine at the national and international levels—as a regional director in 2008, became an officer in 2023, and serves as the board chair through 2027.

“I’m doing the same thing I did from day one: I’m leading by example,” said Roddick. “I represent the wine business. I speak from the heart. I speak authentically about agriculture, jobs, and tourism.”

Roddick may have never gotten into wine if her parents hadn’t encouraged her, as a teenager, to leave a lucrative sales gig at Nordstrom’s in San Jose and go to Cal Poly in 1990. After graduating with degrees in fruit science and agricultural business, she studied Spanish in Cuernavaca, Mexico, then returned to the Central Coast, working in the cellar of regional bubbly pioneer Maison Deutz (now Laetitia). “I dragged hoses,” she said. “I crushed grapes.”

She moved to Paso Robles in 1995, and was hired by Treana winery two years later. When her college classmate Austin Hope walked through the door a month later, she learned his family owned the business. His parents, Chuck and Marlyn Hope, took an immediate liking to Roddick, and asked her to learn the wine business alongside their son. 

“They saw something in me,” said Roddick fondly. “They embraced a journey I had no idea I could be doing. I’m so proud to have been working alongside Austin Hope. We just got up every day and we did it.”

What they did varied widely. Hope Family sold off its first tasting room quickly in order to grow into a national brand, and then returned to focus on the direct-to-consumer experience a decade later. Today, they are all of the above, an international player with two stylish tasting rooms in Paso Robles. Every step of the way, they’ve turned to Roddick to execute Austin’s creative vision. 

“If you don’t know how to do it, Gretchen is not afraid to do it,” Roddick said of how it’s gone for 30 years. “She will figure out a way.”

She wears many hats—promoting Hope Family, Paso Robles, the Central Coast, and California at large—but employs a similar strategy for all. “It’s important to go out and listen,” she said. “We have two ears and one mouth.”

One of her favorite roles is speaking to Cal Poly’s incoming class of wine students. “I speak about their journey and what they can do,” she said. “There’s a place for you. You just gotta find it.”

Roddick clearly found hers, and she’s nowhere near done. “I told Austin, ‘We have 20 more years,’” she said. “There’s a lot to do. We can make a difference. We’re only halfway there.”

title: The Race to Snap Up Grosses Gewächs Rieslings Has Begun. These Are the Bottles to Watch
summary:
Grosses Gewächs (GG), Germany’s equivalent to France's grand cru vineyards, produce bottles that are coveted by collectors around the globe.

The post The Race to Snap Up Grosses Gewächs Rieslings Has Begun. These Are the Bottles to Watch appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At this year’s Grosses Gewächs (GG) preview in Wiesbaden, Germany, the strongest wines carried little evidence of the anxiety behind their production. The 2025 Rieslings were often generous yet energetic, the 2024 reds increasingly individual, and the later releases among the most complete wines on the table.

Germany’s GGs, the dry wines from the country’s highest-ranked vineyards, offer an annual snapshot of the country’s ambitions. This year, they also revealed the nimbleness and flexibility of top German producers. Earlier harvests demanded faster decisions, while increased overall ripeness allowed growers to reconsider typical approaches to balance.

The established names delivered. Alongside them, estates such as Schlumberger-Bernhart, Knewitz, and Rings, as well as those led by younger generations who have taken over family wineries, made a persuasive case for widening the conversation.

The 2025 Rieslings: An Early Reckoning

Of the regions represented, the Mosel and Rheingau were less consistent than I had hoped this year, though their strongest wines remained among the tasting’s highlights.

Florian Lauer, proprietor and winemaker of Weingut Peter Lauer in the Saar, began harvesting on September 7, his earliest yet. He remembers harvests starting in mid-October during his childhood. The shift brings particular difficulties to steep vineyards, where picking cannot simply accelerate to outpace the changing climate.

Compact Riesling bunches are vulnerable to rapidly spreading rot, he explains, while warmer harvest conditions create challenges for a region accustomed to bringing in cooler grapes.

For Matthias Knebel in Winningen, September rain transformed an otherwise steady growing season into a race.

“We started September 15 and finished the harvest in just 16 days,” he says.

At Winningen’s Uhlen vineyard, picking began on September 17 at 102 degrees Oechsle, a German measure of sugar ripeness. 102 degrees is equivalent to an auslese wine, without the influence of botrytis.

“A great blessing of this vintage is the pronounced and energetic acidity, which beautifully supports the ripeness,” says Knebel.

His experience reinforces a growing imperative: once grapes are physiologically ripe, waiting for higher sugar readings risks losing the balance already there.

Lauer is also reconsidering his production methods. His GGs contained less than two grams of residual sugar per liter and underwent full malolactic fermentation. He favors warmer fermentation and savory complexity over overt fruitiness.

“We try to bring out the spiciness,” he says.

His Riesling Kupp showed that approach beautifully, combining clementine and white raspberry flavors with silkiness and flinty detail. Saarfeilser was more savory, with floral complexity and a long, salty finish.

Meanwhile, Clemens Busch’s Marienburg married stone fruit with crunchy freshness, Kühling-Gillot’s Ölberg was expansive and vibrant, and Wittmann’s Aulerde stood out for yellow fruit and a brilliant saline finish. Generosity rarely meant heaviness among the strongest wines.

The Reds: Differences That Matter

The 2024 reds offered considerable quality despite the season’s difficulties. Fürst’s Hundsrück had firm structure and a long future ahead. Meyer-Näkel’s Pfarrwingert brought cherry flavors and silkiness. Franz Keller’s Achkarrer Schlossberg layered black tea, hibiscus, and pomegranate notes, while Rings’ Felsenberg was polished and floral.

As a category, German Pinot Noir can be inconsistent. However, among these producers, quality is largely the starting point.

Beurer’s later-release 2023 Mönchberg Öde Halde illustrated that beautifully, its cherry, raspberry, and red currant unfolding through flowers and spice. The wine’s appeal lay in its ease and detail, with neither acidity nor tannin interrupting its flow.

Cellarmaster Adrien Beurer made adjustments in the winemaking process, including the use of whole bunches, but maintained continuity in the vineyard. “In farming, we didn’t change anything,” he says.

Württemberg also supplied outstanding Lembergers. Schnaitmann’s 2024 Lämmler combined blackberry and sandalwood notes with fresh acidity and substantial but melting tannins, an example of the region’s impressive ambitions.

The 2024 Whites: Worth the Wait

Peter Jakob Kühn releases its GGs a year later than most estates. Its 2024s made an excellent argument for that patience.

“Cool nights brought precision and focus, while balanced rainfall and healthy soils gave natural depth,” says Peter Bernhard Kühn, the winery’s current head.

Kühn’s Mittelheimer St. Nikolaus was rounded and composed, with yellow fruit, flowers, and a stony finish. “It has depth without weight, complexity without excess, and an effortless sense of flow,” Kühn says.

His Hallgartener Jungfer was a highlight for me: flinty, saline, and rounded, with prominent acidity held in remarkable balance.

In Baden, Schlumberger-Bernhart’s cellarmaster Johanna Bernhart also found much to admire.

“2024 was a very wet and cold year, but it provided excellent conditions for cool, mineral-driven white wines,” she says.

Schlumberger-Bernhart’s Altenberg Weingarten Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, and Chardonnay shared freshness and salinity while retaining distinct personalities. The Chardonnay was particularly compelling, with white raspberry and orchard blossom notes, and taut structure.

Odinstal’s unconventional Riesling and Schnaitmann’s electric Götzenberg were also notable. Together, these wines suggested that a GG report is increasingly a story of individual decisions: when to pick, how to ferment, and when to release. The vineyard supplies the possibilities. The grower must recognize which ones the year will allow.

Standout Wines

Peter Lauer Riesling Kupp GG 2025 (Saar)

Lightly flinty, with clementine and white raspberry unfolding across a silky palate. Fine texture and sustained flavor distinguish this beautifully balanced Riesling.

Clemens Busch Riesling Marienburg GG 2025 (Mosel)

Orchard blossom and stone fruit meet a flinty edge. Bright acidity and a crunchy texture bring freshness without diminishing the generous fruit.

Knebel Riesling Uhlen GG 2025 (Mosel)

Generous ripeness meets pronounced, energetic acidity in this refined Riesling. Its concentration is balanced by freshness and elegance.

Kühling-Gillot Riesling Ölberg GG 2025 (Rheinhessen)

A lightly reductive opening reveals white raspberry, papaya, flowers, and exotic spice. Generous in flavor, with flinty detail and mineral vibrancy keeping the palate focused.

Wittmann Riesling Aulerde GG 2025 (Rheinhessen)

Flinty notes frame white raspberry and generous yellow fruit. Expressive and finely balanced, this finishes with pronounced salinity and impressive persistence.

Peter Jakob Kühn Riesling Jungfer GG 2024 (Rheingau)

Flinty reduction introduces a deeply saline Riesling with a rounded, medium-bodied palate. Prominent acidity is beautifully integrated, bringing precision to a wine of considerable texture and depth.

Odinstal Riesling GG 2024 (Pfalz)

Green melon and tangerine candy give this distinctive Riesling an unconventional appeal. Incisive acidity and a crunchy mineral texture keep it lively through the long finish.

Schlumberger-Bernhart Chardonnay Altenberg Weingarten GG 2024 (Baden)

White raspberry and orchard blossom meet flinty notes in this saline, finely balanced Chardonnay. Tension and freshness give the palate particular distinction.

Rudolf Fürst Spätburgunder Hundsrück GG 2024 (Franken)

Pure fruit and floral notes unfold across a rounded palate. Firm tannins and underlying tension give this a substantial framework for aging.

Franz Keller Spätburgunder Schlossberg GG 2024 (Baden)

Black tea, hibiscus, dark cherry, and pomegranate give this Pinot considerable complexity. Supple tannins support the fruit through a long, layered finish.

Rings Spätburgunder Felsenberg GG 2024 (Pfalz)

Elegant and polished, with floral notes and dark berries finely woven together. Baking spice adds detail through a long, composed finish.

Beurer Spätburgunder Mönchberg Öde Halde GG 2023 (Württemberg)

Cherry, raspberry, and red currant mingle with flowers and spice. Elegant and lively, with beautifully integrated acidity and tannins and a long, multilayered finish.

Rainer Schnaitmann Lemberger Lämmler GG 2024 (Württemberg)

Blackberry and black currant meet sandalwood spice in this fresh, expressive red. Substantial but silky tannins provide structure without weighing down the palate.

title: Where to Fly Fish in Wine Country, According to the Pros
summary:
Wine and fly fishing have more in common than you think. Here are the best places to do both.

The post Where to Fly Fish in Wine Country, According to the Pros appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The fishing line unfurls behind you. You gently push your arm and fishing rod forward and let the line unwind. It gracefully lands atop the river without making a ripple. Then, a mouth rises from the water and snatches the fly, you pull back on the line and feel a sharp tug—this is fly fishing.

While nationwide participation remains relatively low, fly fishing is slowly increasing in popularity. According to the American Sportfishing Association’s Special Report on Fishing in 2025, the number of fly fishers in the United States has increased by over 2 million participants compared to a decade prior. 

Any wine lovers interested in exploring fly fishing already have a leg up—the two have more in common than you may think. Finding success on the river requires patience and appreciation for the environment around you, much like enjoying or producing an exceptional bottle of wine. This synergy makes fly fishing in wine country the perfect pairing.

Whether you’re an avid oenophile, a passionate fly fisher, or both, here are some of the best regions to enjoy a glass and hook a giant. 

Please be advised that hiking out to and wading into rivers can be dangerous. Research all regions and bodies of water before heading out. Also, you’ll need a permit to fish in certain rivers.

The Hudson Valley/Catskills, New York

While sometimes disputed, the Catskills, located in Central New York, is often called the birthplace of American fly fishing.

“As it developed in the 1800s, we became the most popular location, and indeed, many of the innovations of those early years occurred in our area,” says Paul T. “Terry” Shultz, a former board member of the Catskill Fly Fishing Center and Museum. Shultz has fished the Catskills since the 1950s.

Early innovators in the region included Theodore Gordon, who revolutionized dry fly fishing (a version where a dry fly sits on the surface of the water instead of sinking); Reuben Cross, who shaped how flies are tied; and Joan Wulff, who reshaped casting techniques and founded a fly fishing school in the Catskills that continues to operate today.

While there’s an abundance of rivers and other bodies of water to fish, some of the best known trout rivers, according to Shultz, include the Beaver Kill, the Willowemoc, the Neversink, the Esopus, and the Schoharie—”these five comprise the ‘Charmed Circle,’” he says. “Plus, the Delaware and its two branches, the East and West.”

About an hour south of the Neversink River, you’ll find the 80-mile-long Shawangunk Wine Trail, which runs throughout Ulster and Orange counties in the Mid-Hudson Valley region and includes 13 wineries and cideries, such as Whitecliff Vineyard, Magnanini Farm Winery, and Angry Orchard’s Cider House.

Lewis-Clark Valley, Idaho

Home to the Snake River, Clearwater River, and more than 50 wineries, Idaho is the place to be for fly fishing wine lovers. Much like the Catskills, the Gem State has a long history with the sport.

“Because of its remoteness and access to high-mountain lakes and streams, Idaho became a fly-fishing destination during the sport’s boom between the 1930s and 1960s,” says Connor Jay Liess, public information specialist at the Idaho Department of Fish and Game. “Well-known public figures such as Ernest Hemingway and even presidents made trips out to Idaho to fish its scenic rivers and streams.”

Idaho is home to three American Viticulture Areas (AVAs): Eagle Foothills, Snake River Valley, and Lewis-Clark Valley. The latter is a favorite of many fly fishers.

“Every year, thousands of folks flock to the Lewis-Clark Valley to fly fish along its scenic rivers and mountain streams,” says Liess. “Lewiston sits in a pretty unique geographic spot in Idaho where the Snake River meets the Clearwater River. Both rivers offer several access sites, spectacular views, and unrivaled opportunities to catch both steelhead and salmon during the colder months, typically September through December.”

Andrew “Drew” Evans, manager at the House of Fly shop in Lewiston, also recommends the Clearwater River for steelhead and notes that fishers can possibly catch smallmouth bass and carp on the Snake River.

While you’re there, be sure to check out the AVA’s eight wineries. Grapes have been planted in the region since at least the 1870s. And the Lewis-Clark AVA produces notable Cabernet Sauvignon, along with Riesling, Tempranillo, and more.

Want to keep the adventure going?

Explore wineries that offer activities here.

Rangeley Lakes Region, Maine

Home to more than 3,000 miles of coastline—one of the largest in the nation—there’s no shortage of places in Maine to explore, especially if fly fishing and wine are on the itinerary.

Michelle Landry, executive director of Historic Rangeley, notes that earliest inhabitants of the Americas and the ancestors of today’s Wabanaki fished Maine’s extensive bodies of water long before European settlers arrived.

But the fishing industry in Maine’s Rangeley region changed in 1863 when George Shepard Page, a businessman from New York, was so “impressed with his Rangeley fishing experience, that he sent eight brook trout he caught to editors of the New York Times, the New York Evening Post, and the Spirit of the Times,” says Landry.

After the “secret was out, more anglers started visiting the Rangeley Lakes region to fish for the famous brook trout,” says Landry. “Hotels, lodges, and sporting camps sprung up around the area to accommodate visitors who wanted to try their hand at catching a record-breaking Maine brook trout.”

For water in Western Maine, Landry notes that the Rapid River, Upper Dam Pool, Magalloway River, Kennebago River, and the Lower Cupsuptic are “known for trophy-size wild brook trout and wild landlocked salmon and are open to fly fishing only,” she says.

After a day on the water, you can check out some of the 15 wineries on the Maine Wine Trail.

“The wine industry is growing exponentially, with new producers and vineyards popping up every year,” says Margot Mazur, wine writer and educator at The Fizz.

But when traveling down the Maine Wine Trail, don’t expect large wineries.

“Maine is mostly made up of smaller vineyards and producers,” says Mazur. “You won’t find many large commercial vineyards in this area, and we’re okay with that. It’s a small community of passionate people and farmers. We’ll be happy to welcome you!”

Grand Junction, Colorado

Home to four national parks and countless miles of river, there’s no shortage of places to explore and get your waders wet in the Centennial State.

If you’re looking to enjoy a glass of something local after a day on the water, head to Grand Junction, Colorado, which is about four hours west of Denver.

Tyler Morris, founder of Drift Boat Taroon Club and a guide at Western Anglers in Grand Junction, leads guided float trips on the lower section of the Colorado River (from Colorado’s Glenwood Springs to Rifle), and a three-day, two-night camping trip down Gunnison Gorge (starting at the Chukar Trail and ending at Pleasure Park).

He notes that the Gunnison is “actually one of the steepest rivers in the continental United States. It’s got the most gradients [and] it’s very, very fast [with] lots of rapids.” So, it’s best to book a guided trip, like with Western Anglers.

While fishing both bodies of water is different, Morris notes that “they’re pretty healthy, wild rivers. There are good wild populations. They don’t stock any of the brown trout. So, every brown trout that you catch is completely wild.”

Along with wild brown trout, you could also possibly catch rainbows, cutthroats, and the Colorado River cutthroat, which is its own subspecies of trout. There are also the native flannelmouth suckers, bluehead suckers, and white fish.

On the stretch of the Colorado River, Morris notes that you can see cottonwood trees, and possibly bald eagles. Whereas on that stretch of the Gunnison, it’s 2,000 feet from the river to the rim of the canyon.

“It’s kind of breathtaking, as corny as that sounds” says Morris. “A lot of people, when we are fishing, I tell them, ‘just take a minute and look up at the canyon walls.’ You’ll see these rock formations that are just so old and just crazy to think that a river formed them.”

Along with ample rivers, Grand Junction is also home to the Grand Valley AVA, where you’ll find more than 30 wineries. While a host of grapes are planted throughout the state, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, and Riesling are the dominant varieties.

title: This Chic Roman Bar Is Basically an Art Museum with Cocktails
summary:
Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace is an art history lover’s dream, without the tickets and crowds of most Roman haunts.

The post This Chic Roman Bar Is Basically an Art Museum with Cocktails appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The amount of art to see in Rome is overwhelming. Over 20 Caravaggio paintings hang in churches, museums, and palaces scattered throughout the city. The Sistine Chapel awaits only those who sweat through an hours-long queue (or pay fees to skip the line.) But one unassuming yet glamorous bar, in the lobby of a hotel perched on the city’s highest hilltop, is a museum in and of itself.

With three masterpieces from Giovanni Battista Tiepolo and countless rare paintings, sculptures, furniture, and tapestries, Rome Cavalieri’s Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace is an art history lover’s dream, without the tickets and crowds of most Roman haunts.

Even if you’re not staying overnight in one of the hotel’s palatial suites, many of which house art themselves—an original painting from Andy Warhol’s Dollar Sign series hangs in the penthouse—you can visit Tiepolo for aperitivo and soak in all the art history. The ornate, elegant bar is open to the public and even hosts tours guided by local art historians.

The Decor

Rome Cavalieri, a Waldorf Astoria hotel, houses one of the more impressive private art collections in the world, with over a thousand rare and historic pieces displayed throughout the hotel. The most notable paintings hang near the lobby’s elegant Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace, named after the three Giovanni Battista Tiepolo masterpieces displayed on the wall beside the bar. Known for his frescoes and Rococo style, the Venice-born artist is considered one of the most important painters of the 18th century.

The three large canvases—the only pieces at Rome Cavalieri behind glass, due to their preciousness—include “Odysseus finds Achilles among the daughters of Lycomedes,” “The Flaying of Marsyas,” and “Hercules and Antaeus.”

Secure your spot now.

Guests can sip their aperitivo from the cozy antique furniture that surrounds the sleek bar while gazing upon the 18th-century Tiepolo paintings, or the large tapestry of “L’Histoire de l’Empereur de Chine,” replicas of which hang at the Louvre, the Met, and the Getty Museum. Frequent live harp and piano performances elevate the classic atmosphere even further, and terrace seating offers sweeping views of the hotel’s Mediterranean gardens and the Rome cityscape.

The Drinks

In addition to all the aperitivo classics you would expect from a Roman bar—spritzes, martinis, and bitter sodas abound—the Tiepolo menu features a thoughtful collection of art-inspired cocktails that take cues from the property’s most prominent works. The signature Tiepolo cocktail is an aromatic, gently bitter gin and grapefruit treat, while A…Dollar, inspired by the penthouse’s original Warhol, is a vanilla-scented vodka sour riff. 

There is also an impressive assortment of zero-proof options, as well, including my personal favorite, the refreshing Vermeil 0%, made with Sabatini 0% gin and herbal Tassoni cedrata soda. Between 3:30 and 5:30 p.m., the lounge offers a dedicated high tea service, with finger sandwiches and freshly baked sweet treats like madeleines and mini plum cakes.

The Crowd

Expect to see relaxed guests enjoying a glamorous pre-dinner aperitivo, or more casual business meetings over coffee (or high tea service) earlier in the day. The bar is open to the general public and typically has ample seating available without reservations. 

The Bottom Line

For world-famous art with top-tier cocktails to match, Tiepolo Lounge and Terrace offers a singular experience in Rome. Despite the seriousness of the surrounding artwork, Tiepolo feels welcoming, warm, and relaxed.

Why Portugal Is One of the World’s Most Exciting Wine Regions

What wine should you open with dinner? The answer, regardless of what’s on the table, is Portuguese.

Within the country’s confines, you can find a whole globe of styles to match every meal, be it large or small, snack-y or stretched into several courses. With over 250 native grape varieties and a wild diversity of wine regions, Portuguese wines have range.

“In a wine world that often speaks through a familiar handful of international varieties, Portugal has preserved an entire native vocabulary,” says Master Sommelier June Rodil, partner and CEO of Goodnight Hospitality. “Arinto’s salt, citrus, and electric acidity; Encruzado’s layered, quietly powerful texture; Touriga Nacional’s perfume and architecture; Baga’s yummy yet haunting, savory grip.”

The Rich Diversity of Portuguese Wine

The expressive red wines of the Douro Valley complement savory dishes like grilled tuna steak, spiced curry, or winter braises. In the summer months, brighter reds made from the Baga grape, grown on Bairrada’s coast, or Castelão from the hills outside Lisboa play well with low-key pizzas, grilled skewers, or platters of cheeses, olives, and meats. 

Touriga Nacional, arguably Portugal’s most iconic grape, is revered for its structure and elegant perfumes. In the Douro, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinta Amerela (i.e. Trincadeira), and Touriga Franca all offer their own unique brand of liveliness, structure, and spice to blends.

Freshness-seekers have a lot to love in the country’s white varieties. Found both in blends and single-variety wines, the vibrant acidity of the Arinto grape or the aromatic character of Loureiro, which hails from the North West, cut through the crunch of fried fritters and elevate crisp salad. Globally-popular Alvarinho is known for precision and intensity, while Encruzado, found in the Dão, brings texture to a blend. 

“These grapes can be beautiful on their own, but many are at their most compelling in a convo with one another, building complexity through contrast rather than sheer weight,” says Rodil. 

Portugal’s excellence goes well beyond still reds and whites. The sparkling wines of Bairrada are full of energy and an oceanic acidity. And of course, Port, one of the world’s most iconic wines, and Madeira, a fortified island wine, need little introduction.

This variety of styles, native grapes, and expressions mean that there’s a whole country to discover. And more wine stories to unravel around every corner. 

“You aren’t tasting a Portuguese grape trying to fit a global mold; you’re tasting place, history, and personality, all speaking with a distinctly Portuguese accent,” Rodil adds.

Structured Reds of the Douro

The extreme, rugged slopes of the Douro Valley is home to hundreds of unique varieties and an extensive array of old vines. From the slopes and xisto (schist) soil surrounding the river come wines of structure, power, and finesse. 

Touriga Nacional—one of Portugal’s most emblematic varieties—brings aromatics and concentration to the Douro’s signature red blends. Other indigenous red grapes like Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, and Tinta Amarela all add their own unique characteristics to the mix. Their diverse aromas and textures give winemakers space to play and to build the perfect blend.

Expressive Alentejo

While the Douro’s landscapes are dramatic, Alentejo is mostly a region of gently rolling plains dotted with oak and cork trees. An overarching quality of both the reds and whites is freshness—surprising considering the sundrenched summer days that bless the region. 

With a 2,000-year-old history of viticulture, Alentejo is home to a number of beloved varieties. Alicante Bouschet is the star in the region’s iconic red blends. Aragonez (Tempranillo) brings structure and elegance. Juicy Castelão is often added into blends for its red fruit aromas. Likewise, Trincadeira, for its plummy, savory notes, while Moreto is recognized for its low acidity and nuttiness. And Arinto brings lemon-lime brightness to refreshing white blends.

Refreshing Vinhos Verdes

The salty Atlantic air and the cool ocean breezes make the Vinhos Verdes wine region one of the most distinctive growing areas in Portugal. White grapes, including Alvarinho, Arinto (Pedernã, to the locals), Azal, Avesso, Loureiro, and Trajadura is blended into aromatic, fresh, verdant wines that shine when paired with seafood or dishes with big spice, bright citrus, or an herbaceous kick.

Elegant Dão

Surrounded by mountains in all directions, Dão is one of the oldest regions in Portugal. Touriga Nacional, the region’s star, brings to life age-worthy blends with full body and great alcohol content. Open a bottle with a rib-eye or cold-weather braises, like Caçoila, a warming stewed beef dish. 

Don’t overlook the region’s other grapes. Tinta Pinheira, also known as Rufete, has an incredible depth of color and complexity. Encruzado, a noble white grape, with lively lemon aromas.

Bouncy Bairrada

Hugging the coast and defined by Atlantic influence, Bairrada is known for its cool, sea-kissed climate.

Two styles shine here: the fierce tannins and springy saltiness of single-variety Baga, with its wild fruit and early minerality, and Portuguese’s finest sparkling wines, born from centuries-old vines in sandy soils by the sea and bursting with tension, aromatics, and ocean salinity.

Beyond Baga and bubbles, white grapes like Fernão Pires (or, Maria Gomes), Arinto, Bical, and Cercial tend to take on a striking mineral character.

Surfer Cool Lisboa

Lisboa’s wines are made between the cool winds of the Atlantic ocean and the sunny heat of inland Portugal. Sun and surf define wines—maritime influence, morning fog, ocean breezes, and white wines full of seaside minerality. Reds range from structured and powerful to easy-drinking and beachy. That vibrant acidity will cut through fat and spice—be it from pho or larb, or comfy Southern flavors.

Península de Setúbal

One of the country’s most prestigious regions is also the birthplace of Moscatel de Setúbal, a rich, aromatic fortified sweet wine. With a richly Mediterranean climate, the red wines of the Palmela region, based on the Castelão grape variety, have complexity, depth, and extreme ageability.

“Portuguese wine can move through an entire menu, from something bracing and oceanic to something structured and deeply soulful, while remaining unmistakably itself,” Rodil adds. “For a sommelier, that range is what makes these wines so badass.”

title: Collecting Chartreuse Is a Spiritual Contradiction. Somms Do It Anyway
summary:
Chartreuse sustains the lives of the monks who make it, yet they refuse to exploit its value fully. Still, the liqueur inspires a frenzy among collectors.

The post Collecting Chartreuse Is a Spiritual Contradiction. Somms Do It Anyway appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At the end of a great wine dinner, when the bottles stand empty and the table has fallen into the pleasant disorder of stained glasses and dismantled cheese plates, Paul Einbund reaches for Chartreuse.

“I can be completely taken by the wines, but when I pour Chartreuse afterward, I remember how deeply it affects me,” says Einbund. He’s the owner of San Francisco restaurants The Morris and Sirene, as well as the coauthor, with Jordan Mackay, of the forthcoming Little Green Book of Chartreuse. “Made from 130 herbs and plants, it’s just more complex than anything else. There is mystery and drama in the glass!”

For years, this was Einbund’s private passion, when all Chartreuse did was gather dust on liquor store shelves, and many dismissed it as an eccentric digestif or a formidable ingredient in old cocktails. Then bartenders rediscovered drinks such as the Last Word, and sommeliers began pouring vintage bottles after dinner. Soon the spirits world’s trending fascination grew into something approaching mania.

From Mythic Origins to Collector Obsession

Chartreuse begins with 130 plants, herbs, roots, barks, seeds, and spices. Around half, by volume, come from the French and Italian Alps, according to Philippe Rochez, sales director of Chartreuse Diffusion. Others arrive from farther away. All are delivered dried to the Grande Chartreuse monastery in France, where secrecy is maintained with almost theatrical rigor.

Only two monks know the complete recipe and its precise proportions. A third knows the ingredients and inspects each shipment as it arrives. Before passing the invoices to the accountant, this monk uses a black marker to obscure what has been ordered. The company may pay for the plants and spices, but its accountants are not permitted to know what they are.

The monks combine the botanicals inside the monastery, placing them into coded bags before they are sent for distillation. Different proportions and methods produce Green Chartreuse, Yellow Chartreuse, and the powerful Élixir Végétal. The liqueurs are sweetened with French beet sugar and aged in oak vessels ranging from barriques to enormous vats. Chartreuse Diffusion buys new barrels to avoid foreign aromas and refuses to sell retired ones for use by other producers.

Time brings the alcohol, sugar, and plants together. Older Green Chartreuse can evoke pine, smoke, tea, and peppercorn. Yellow, made at a lower strength and with different proportions, can turn toward ginger, cardamom, saffron, and dried fruit.

This complexity helps explain its appeal to sommeliers. Einbund considers Chartreuse through much the same framework he applies to wine: weight, acidity, balance, intensity, and density. He drinks it differently, however.

“Because of the higher alcohol levels, I sip by taking a little more than wetting my lips, and I almost let it evaporate on my palate,” he says. “This way I can slow things down and watch the flavors expand as I enjoy them, and avoid the burn at the same time.”

Its evolution in bottle has also created a passionate collector culture. Vintage-spirits consultant Seth Weinberg began accumulating Chartreuse after tasting several releases together. “Many years ago after trying multiple vintages of Chartreuse side by side, I noticed the nuanced differences in various vintages,” Weinberg says. “This realization led to a natural urge to collect.”

His approach resembles building a wine cellar: buy each release when it appears, then wait. “Since Chartreuse ages like a wine in the bottle, I believe it is paramount to buy bottles when they are released, and age them for many years for the flavors to develop, oxidize, and harmonize,” he says.

The trophies include a 1953 VEP made to commemorate the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, the original ninth-centenary bottling from 1984, and a three-liter carbon-fiber Jeroboam released in 2019 and limited to 999 bottles. Weinberg bought the Jeroboam at the distillery in France and carried it throughout the country, its weight wearing down the rubber on his suitcase wheels against the cobblestones.

Yet collecting Chartreuse contains a spiritual contradiction. The Carthusians do not live on donations. They support themselves through their work, with revenue through Chartreuse Diffusion helping sustain the order and its monasteries. They make liqueur to preserve their independence and a life devoted to silence, solitude, and prayer—not to build a global liquor empire.

The Mystery and Mythology of a Sacred Spirit

“All winemakers like Chartreuse,” says Rochez, who has spent 38 years at Chartreuse Diffusion, his first and only employer. He sees a kinship between winegrowers and the monks. Both work with plants, depend upon nature, and allow time to finish what they began. Climate change is complicating that work, Rochez says, as some herbs become drier and others more difficult to source.

Chartreuse’s history has demanded similar patience. The liqueur takes its name from the Chartreuse Mountains, where Saint Bruno founded the Carthusian order in 1084. The Carthusians received a manuscript for an “elixir of long life” in 1605 and spent more than 150 years refining it. The liqueur survived revolution; the monks’ expulsion from France; production in Tarragona, Spain; the destruction of the distillery in Fourvoirie, France; and periods when few people seemed to want it.

Einbund believes the enigma and mythology surrounding Chartreuse is central to its hold over sommeliers. Wine professionals spend their lives studying provenance, production, and vintage, but Chartreuse keeps part of itself hidden. 

“One of the most important lessons for me about Chartreuse is to let go of trying to be right, or know everything,” he says. “Chartreuse is a mystery and always will be. That’s part of what makes it so amazing.”

Demand for Chartreuse began surging during the cocktail renaissance of the early 2000s, fueled by the revival of the Last Word, and accelerated further with the rise of home mixology during the pandemic. But the monks refused to keep increasing production simply because the market would absorb it. According to Rochez, they now make more Chartreuse than they did for much of the past several decades, but have stabilized output to protect their monastic life.

Bottles consequently disappear, allocations tighten, and prices climb. What once gathered dust is now hoarded, traded, and displayed behind glass. This troubles the monks, who believe Chartreuse should be opened and shared, not treated as a speculative asset.

Weinberg understands the contradiction. “I share the same sentiment as the monks,” he says. “Bottles of liquor are best enjoyed when opened and shared.”

Perhaps this is what sommeliers recognize most clearly. Every extraordinary bottle arrives with the knowledge that opening it destroys the object that has been guarded. Chartreuse asks for that surrender more forcefully than most. Conceived as an “elixir of long life,” it now sustains the lives of the monks who make it, yet they refuse to exploit its value fully. They will produce enough to preserve their way of life, but not enough to satisfy our appetite. 

Back at Einbund’s table, poured after the last wine, its purpose becomes clear. Chartreuse slows the evening down, giving its flavors and the conversation around them time to expand. Perhaps that is why it affects him so deeply: The liqueur was never meant to live behind glass, but among the people gathered around it.

Celebrate Fall with a Four-Course Italian Alpine Dinner Party

A taste of Trentino, without leaving home.

Imagine an autumn evening in the Italian Alps: crisp mountain air, a full table of seasonal dishes, toasting friends, a complete sense of presence. Make that vision a reality with this Italian Alpine Dinner Party.

Rooted in the dramatic landscapes of Trentino, Italy, where vineyards climb the foothills of the Dolomites and cool alpine conditions preserve freshness and acidity, Mezzacorona and Rotari wines capture the freshness, elegance, and distinctive character of their region. 

These wines take center stage across an inspired four-course, fall menu. Each pairing brings something different to the table, starting with the Rotari Brut and Rotari Brut Rosé, both crafted in the Alps using the traditional bottle-fermentation technique that gives the lively sparkling wines their fine bubbles, freshness, complexity, and refined texture.  The experience then moves into the still wines of Trentino, from the fresh, mineral precision of Domenica Pinot Grigio to the juicy, expressive character of DiNotte Red Blend

Consider this your invitation to slow down, savor each glass, and enjoy the Italian art of gathering one delicious course at a time.

Explore the Wines

Welcome Aperitivo

Rotari Brut Trentodoc

Apple & Radicchio Bruschetta

Elegant, crisp, and vibrant, Rotari Brut sets a celebratory tone for the evening with its fine bubbles, notes of citrus, and warm aromas. A Trentodoc crafted using the classic method, Rotari Brut reflects the character of Trentino’s vineyards, where high altitudes and cool mountain conditions help preserve the freshness that define the region’s sparkling wines. Its lively acidity pairs effortlessly with crispy apple and bitter radicchio, creating a refreshing first bite to welcome your guests into your home.

Bursting with red fruit and delicate mountain minerality, Rotari Brut Rosé brings a vibrant, colorful expression of Trentodoc to the first course. Made with Pinot Nero and Chardonnay, the blend’s bright acidity cuts through the rich pancetta and sweet pumpkin of this bold and slightly bitter salad.

This layered pairing balances richness and allows DiNotte’s lush fruitiness to shine alongside the layered savory notes of the dish.

title: With Over 100,000 Bottles, This Basque Cellar Is Like a Museum for Wine Lovers
summary:
